title: Upamanyu asks Shiva for milk
hookLine: a hungry boy asks Shiva for milk, and the Rudram's companion asks for rice and lentils
carry: asking shiva for ordinary needs is devotion too
tomorrow: Why Hindus bathe the Shiva linga

cards: A small boy named Upamanyu, from a poor family of forest hermits, sees another child drinking milk, and runs home to ask for some. His mother has none. So she stirs a little flour into water and hands it to him.
He takes one sip and knows. This isn't milk. And his mother, in the Mahabharata's telling, says the honest thing: people like us only get milk by Shiva's grace.
So the boy decides to ask Shiva himself.

teach.h: FROM SHIVA, OR FROM NO ONE.
teach.b: He goes to the mountains and prays with his whole small body. A god appears, looking like Indra on his great elephant, and offers him anything at all, if he'll stop asking Shiva.
Upamanyu says no: from Shiva, or from no one. Then the disguise falls away. It was Shiva, testing him, and Shiva gives him milk without end, and something better, a devotion that never leaves him.
Notice what the boy asked for. Not freedom from the world. Milk.
This is a real Hindu teaching: asking God for ordinary needs is part of devotion, not beneath it.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names four kinds of people who come to him, among them the one in trouble and the one who wants something in this world, and he calls all of them good.

The Rudram has a companion that says it in a list. When it's chanted in full, the bowing half, the Namakam, is paired with the Chamakam, where line after line ends in two small words: cha me, and to me.
Strength, and to me. Ease, and what is dear. Milk and ghee and honey.

teach.h: RICE, LENTILS, RAIN, A SHARED MEAL.
teach.b: Rice and barley, beans and sesame, wheat and lentils. Plowing, and rain.
And eating together, and drinking together. Many teachers hear the pair like breathing. The Namakam breathes out: everything is Rudra's.
The Chamakam breathes in: from all that, may this come to me.

how: When the Shri Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the Namakam with the Chamakam, and both are recited in Vedic Sanskrit, at home, in temples and during abhishekam.

o: a boy who asked Shiva for milk, and wasn't scolded
a boy told that asking God for food is shameful
a hymn that forbids asking a god for anything at all

games.q: the boy and the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the boy who asked Shiva for milk
built on cha me, and to me

s: Upamanyu's mother gave him flour stirred into water
he tasted it and knew it wasn't milk.
in the Gita, only the wise are welcome to come to God
Krishna names four kinds, including the one in trouble and the one who wants something, and calls all of them good.
the Chamakam asks only for spiritual gifts
it asks for rice, barley, lentils, rain, and eating together too.

games.q: a god offers Upamanyu anything he wants, if he'll stop asking Shiva. what does the boy say?
o: yes: milk is milk, whoever gives it.
no: from Shiva, or from no one.
he takes the gift and keeps asking Shiva too.
games.why: the god was Shiva in disguise, testing him. the boy kept asking the one he loved, and got milk and a lifelong devotion.

practice: Without judging the list, let a few plain needs come up, not big wishes but ordinary things: sleep, a good meal, someone to eat it with, rain if your garden is dry.
Name each one quietly and hold it out, the way the Chamakam does, then let the list go on the out-breath.
If you pray, offer these needs to Shiva in your own words, the way Upamanyu asked for milk; if you don't, just name them honestly.

wordCard.voice: The Rudram. Today, its companion, the Chamakam: cha me, and to me, asking plainly for grain, rain, and company at the table.

orig.note: Sanskrit: and to me. the refrain of the Chamakam.

carryVoice: Your line: asking Shiva for ordinary needs is devotion too. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Krishna tells Upamanyu's story: flour in water for milk, austerity to Shiva, Shiva tests him in Indra's form, then grants him milk and lasting devotion)
Bhagavad Gita 7.16–7.18 (four kinds of people worship me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, the wise; all are noble)
Taittiriya Samhita 4.7 (Chamakam: requests ending cha me, including strength, ease, food, grains, plowing and rain, eating and drinking together)
Taittiriya Samhita 4.5 (Namakam, for the contrast with namah)
